content: Palpation of the precordium involves placing the palm of the hand on the anterior chest wall to evaluate the size of the heart, detect the presence of a heave or lifting of the chest, and assess for a thrill or turbulent blood flow. The point of maximum impulse (PMI) is typically located at or near the 5th intercostal space along the mid-clavicular line. In obese patients or those with hyperinflated lungs, such as in emphysema, the apex of the heart may be difficult to palpate. If the apex is not easily felt, the search should extend laterally and inferiorly to check for cardiomegaly, which can significantly displace the PMI. If no impulse is found on the left side of the chest after a thorough search, the right side should be examined to rule out dextrocardia. The PMI should be described using the mnemonic SALID: S (Size): Is it larger than one interspace? A (Amplitude): Is it weak or diminished? L (Location): Is it located in the 5th intercostal space at the mid-clavicular line? I (Impulse): Is it monophasic or biphasic? D (Duration): Is it abnormally sustained? The apex beat is best described as the most lateral and most inferior point of apex pulsation. A heave is felt as an upward displacement of the chest against the hand and is best detected using the heel of the hand placed along the sternal border. A thrill is a palpable murmur that feels similar to a cat purring. The fingertips are often more sensitive to this vibration. Thrills are caused by turbulent blood flow, often due to valvular abnormalities. For example, thrills from aortic stenosis are best felt near the right upper sternal border. If a loud murmur is detected during auscultation, reassess for the presence of a thrill. Thrills are generally an uncommon finding. When palpating the precordium in a female patient, place the palm of your right hand directly beneath the patient’s left breast, ensuring that the edge of your index finger rests against the inferior surface of the breast. Always explain to the patient what you are about to do and why before performing this maneuver. Keep in mind that with age, tissue turgor often decreases, causing the breasts to hang below the level of the heart. The normal-sized and functioning left ventricle generates a penny-sized impulse that is best felt in the mid-clavicular line at the 5th intercostal space. If the ventricle becomes dilated, often due to past infarctions and associated with ventricular dysfunction, the PMI is displaced laterally. In cases of significant enlargement, the PMI may be located near the axilla. Occasionally, the PMI may not localize to a specific area, which does not necessarily indicate ventricular enlargement or dysfunction. Obesity and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) can also limit the ability to identify the precise location of the PMI. Palpating while the patient is in the left lateral decubitus position can make the PMI more apparent. The duration of the impulse, which refers to how long the impulse is felt, is a subjective finding and can be challenging to detect. Note that hypertrophy and dilation are not synonymous; they can occur independently or together. The vigor of the transmitted impulse can vary. For example, conditions such as compensated mitral regurgitation or aortic insufficiency, which result in exceptionally large stroke volumes, can produce an unusually forceful impulse. Finally, assess for thrills, which are vibratory sensations caused by turbulent blood flow, often secondary to valvular abnormalities. The sensation is similar to the vibration felt when partially obstructing the flow of water through a garden hose. For instance, thrills caused by aortic stenosis are best felt near the right upper sternal border. If a loud murmur is detected during auscultation, reassess for a thrill. However, thrills are generally uncommon findings.
